1281.event_title: Crown Prince Akihito meets Shōda Michiko on a Karuizawa tennis court
1281.event: In August 1957 Japan’s Crown Prince Akihito met Shōda Michiko, the daughter of a flour-milling company president, on a tennis court in the mountain resort of Karuizawa. The two kept meeting over games of tennis, and in April 1959 they married, breaking a long tradition: she was the first commoner to marry a Japanese crown prince. The romance set off a wave of public enthusiasm in Japan, including a national craze for tennis.
1281.explanation: A courtship that began simply with seeing each other across a tennis net became one of the most celebrated royal marriages of the twentieth century.
1281.tie_back: The kural says love, unlike wine, brings joy just by seeing and thinking of the beloved, and this romance grew out of nothing more than repeated meetings on a tennis court.
1281._accuracy_note: Next-best: a well-documented love that began with simply seeing each other, but the sources record the meeting and marriage, not the inner joy of mere sight that the kural describes.

1282.event_title: Young Gandhi’s jealous quarrels with Kasturba
1282.date: 1880s (early years of their marriage, which began in 1882)
1282.event: Mohandas Gandhi and Kasturba were married in 1882, when both were about thirteen. In his autobiography, in the chapter Playing the Husband, Gandhi wrote that he soon became a jealous husband without any reason to suspect her, and insisted that she could not go anywhere without his permission. Kasturba did not accept these restrictions, and Gandhi recalled that the two child-spouses often ended up refusing to speak to each other; he later called her innocent in taking liberties with his rules and admitted his strictness had been misguided.
1282.explanation: Gandhi himself presented these quarrels as the foolishness of a young husband whose petty suspicions were out of all proportion to the bond between them, a bond that lasted the rest of their lives.
1282.tie_back: The kural says that when love is as tall as a palmyra palm one should not sulk even as much as a millet seed, and Gandhi looked back on his small-minded jealous sulks as exactly that kind of mistake.
1282._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: it shows small quarrels set against a large love, though the sulking was mostly the husband’s jealousy rather than the lovers’ pique the kural has in mind; the quarrels are known chiefly from Gandhi’s own account.

1283.event_title: Sofya Tolstaya at the window of the stationmaster’s house at Astapovo
1283.place: Astapovo railway station, Ryazan province, Russia
1283.event: In late October 1910 the 82-year-old Leo Tolstoy secretly left his estate at Yasnaya Polyana, leaving behind his wife Sofya, to whom he had been married for 48 years. He fell ill with pneumonia on the journey and lay dying in the stationmaster’s house at the small railway station of Astapovo. Sofya rushed there, but in keeping with his wishes his followers kept her out; she paced the platform and tried to look in through the windows, watched by photographers and film crews, and was allowed to his side only at the very end.
1283.explanation: Though her husband had walked out on her without a word of farewell, Sofya could not stay away and could not stop trying to see him.
1283.tie_back: The kural’s wife says that even if her husband slights her and does as he pleases, her eyes cannot rest without seeing him, which is almost exactly what the world watched Sofya Tolstaya do at Astapovo.
1283._accuracy_note: Very strong: a neglected wife whose eyes cannot rest without seeing her husband is nearly a dramatisation of the kural, though the marriage behind it was far more troubled than the poem’s.

1284.event_title: Napoleon locks his door on Joséphine, then forgives her
1284.place: Rue de la Victoire, Paris, France
1284.event: After seventeen months away on the Egyptian expedition, Napoleon Bonaparte returned secretly to France in the autumn of 1799, angry at reports about his wife Joséphine’s conduct in his absence. Joséphine had driven south to meet him and missed him on the road, and when she reached their house in Paris he kept his bedroom door locked against her despite hours of pleading and tears, joined by her children Hortense and Eugène. In the end he let her in and they were fully reconciled, to the annoyance of his family.
1284.explanation: Napoleon had come home determined to stay cold, but his resolve gave way almost at once.
1284.tie_back: The kural describes a heart that set out to sulk but forgot it and went straight toward reunion; Napoleon’s locked door, opened within a day or two, shows the same collapse of a planned sulk.
1284._accuracy_note: Strong illustration of a planned sulk giving way to reconciliation, though here it is the husband who sulks and the wife’s pleading, not only his own heart, that ends it.

1285.event_title: Ulysses S. Grant tells Julia to keep the eyes he fell in love with
1285.event: Julia Dent Grant had strabismus (crossed eyes) all her life and was self-conscious about it, especially once her husband became famous during the Civil War. In late 1863 she asked the St. Louis surgeon Charles Pope about an operation to straighten her eyes and was told it was too late. In her memoirs she recorded that when she told her husband, Ulysses S. Grant told her he had fallen in love with her with those same eyes, liked them as they were, and did not want her to change them.
1285.explanation: Grant simply did not see as a flaw what Julia feared made her a plain wife for a great man.
1285.tie_back: The kural says that just as the eye cannot see the kohl brush touching it, the lover cannot see the beloved’s faults when close to them, and Grant could not see his wife’s squint as a fault at all.
1285._accuracy_note: Strong: love that does not see the beloved’s supposed flaw is the kural’s exact point, though it is the husband, not the wife, who is blind to the fault, and the exact words survive only in Julia’s memoir.

1286.event_title: Einstein and Mileva Marić: love letters, then bitterness at a distance
1286.event: Albert Einstein and Mileva Marić met as students at the Federal Polytechnic in Zürich, and 54 surviving letters from 1897 to shortly after their marriage in 1903 show a warm romance carried on while they were often apart. Einstein married her in 1903 despite his parents’ strong objections. The couple separated in 1914, when Mileva lived in Zürich and Einstein in Berlin, divorced in 1919, and their communication afterwards was often bitter.
1286.explanation: The same couple whose early letters overflowed with affection came, once living apart for good, to see mainly each other’s faults.
1286.tie_back: The kural speaks of seeing no faults in the beloved when together and nothing but faults when apart, and the Einstein letters trace a love that turned toward grievance once distance became permanent.
1286._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the kural describes a passing mood of a loving wife, while this is the slow breakdown of a marriage; the link between distance and fault-finding is an interpretation, not something the sources state.

1287.event_title: Edward VIII abdicates to marry Wallis Simpson
1287.event: King Edward VIII had fallen in love with the American Wallis Simpson, and in 1936 it became clear he was determined to marry her once her divorce was final. The government, the Church of England, the opposition parties and the Dominions would not accept a twice-divorced woman as queen, and Edward came to see that he had to choose between the crown and her. On 10 December 1936 he signed an Instrument of Abdication, which took legal effect the next day, and he married Wallis Simpson in France on 3 June 1937.
1287.explanation: Edward chose the woman he loved over the throne, knowing in advance that the marriage could not be reconciled with remaining king.
1287.tie_back: The kural asks what use it is to resist when one already knows the current will sweep one away, like those who leap into a flood knowing it will carry them off; Edward’s love carried him over the edge of the throne with his eyes open.
1287._accuracy_note: Next-best: it shows love as a current one knowingly yields to, but the kural is about the futility of a lover’s sulk, not about giving up a crown.

1288.event_title: Frida Kahlo and Diego Rivera remarry in San Francisco
1288.event: The Mexican painters Frida Kahlo and Diego Rivera married in 1929, but their marriage was strained by a series of extramarital affairs, notably Rivera’s with Kahlo’s younger sister, and they divorced in 1939. In late 1940 Kahlo travelled to San Francisco, where Rivera was working for the Golden Gate International Exposition, and the two reconciled. They remarried there on 8 December 1940, barely a year after their divorce.
1288.explanation: Despite the real and public hurt Rivera had caused her, Kahlo could not stay away from him.
1288.tie_back: The kural’s wife calls her husband a thief and says that though he brings her shameful pain, his embrace is to her what wine is to the drinker who keeps craving more, which fits Kahlo’s return to Rivera after all he had done.
1288._accuracy_note: Strong: a wife drawn back to a husband who had caused her humiliating pain is close to the kural, though the sources record the remarriage, not her feelings about it.

1289.event_title: Wagner wakes Cosima with the Siegfried Idyll
1289.event: Richard Wagner secretly composed a gentle piece for small orchestra as a birthday present for his new wife, Cosima. On Christmas morning 1870, when they were to celebrate her birthday, a small group of musicians directed by Wagner played it on the stairs outside her bedroom to wake her. The piece, first named after their home at Tribschen, became known as the Siegfried Idyll, after their young son.
1289.explanation: Wagner, known for vast and stormy operas, chose an intimate, quiet gesture for the right moment.
1289.tie_back: The kural says love is more delicate than a flower and few grasp its perfect moment; the Siegfried Idyll is a rare documented case of a lover choosing exactly the right, tender moment to express love.
1289._accuracy_note: Next-best: it illustrates delicacy and good timing in love, but the kural is a general reflection on how few understand love’s tender nature, which no single event can show fully.

1290.event_title: Eleanor of Castile goes on crusade with Edward
1290.place: Acre, Kingdom of Jerusalem (now in Israel)
1290.event: In August 1270 the future Edward I of England set out on crusade to the Holy Land, and his wife Eleanor of Castile went with him instead of staying behind. They reached Acre in 1271, and their daughter Joan, known as Joan of Acre, was born there about a year later. Eleanor travelled with Edward until 1273; the popular story that she saved his life by sucking poison from a dagger wound is regarded as legend.
1290.explanation: Rather than wait years at home, Eleanor chose to share a long and dangerous journey so as not to be parted from her husband.
1290.tie_back: The kural’s husband says his wife was even more eager than he for their embrace, and Eleanor’s choice to follow Edward across the world shows a wife whose eagerness for togetherness outran convention.
1290._accuracy_note: Next-best only: it shows a wife eager not to be separated, but nothing in the sources matches the kural’s scene of a glance of displeasure melting into an embrace.
